Pan-Seared Salmon with Lemon Beurre Blanc
Restaurant-quality salmon with perfectly crispy skin and a silky French butter sauce. Easier than it looks, impressive every time.
Pan-seared salmon fillet with crispy skin and lemon butter sauce
Remove salmon from refrigerator 15-20 minutes before cooking. Pat completely dry with paper towels—this is crucial for crispy skin. Season generously with salt and pepper on both sides.
Dry fish = crispy skin. Wet fish = steamed, soggy skin.
Start the beurre blanc: In a small saucepan, combine wine, shallot, and vinegar over medium heat. Simmer until reduced to about 2 tablespoons, about 5-7 minutes.
Add the cream to the reduction and simmer for 1 minute. Remove from heat.
Add the cold butter one cube at a time, whisking constantly. Don't add the next cube until the previous one is almost fully incorporated. The sauce should be creamy and emulsified, not oily.
Keep the sauce barely warm. Too hot and it will break. If it starts to separate, add an ice cube and whisk vigorously.
Stir in lemon juice, lemon zest, and chives. Season with salt to taste. Keep warm (not hot) while you cook the salmon.
Heat a large stainless steel or cast iron skillet over medium-high heat until very hot, about 2-3 minutes. Add the oil and swirl to coat.
Place salmon fillets skin-side down in the pan. Press gently with a spatula for the first 30 seconds to ensure good contact with the pan. Don't move the fish.
Cook for 4-5 minutes without touching, until the skin is deeply golden and crispy. You'll see the salmon cooking up the sides—when it's about 3/4 of the way up, flip.
Flip and cook for 2-3 minutes more for medium (slightly translucent in the center) or 4 minutes for well done.
Remove from heat and let rest for 1 minute. Serve immediately with the beurre blanc spooned over or alongside.
Beurre blanc can be made up to 2 hours ahead and kept warm in a thermos. If it breaks, blend with an immersion blender while adding a tablespoon of cold cream.

We tested this with both wild and farmed salmon. Wild salmon (especially sockeye) has less fat, so reduce cook time by 1 minute per side. We also tested making the sauce with salted butter—it works, but reduce or eliminate the added salt at the end.

The key to beurre blanc is temperature control. The sauce is an emulsion—cold butter whisked into warm (not hot) liquid. If your pan is too hot, the butter will melt into oil rather than emulsifying into a creamy sauce. If this happens, don't panic: add an ice cube and whisk aggressively to bring it back.

Pan-seared salmon with beurre blanc is one of those dishes that defines restaurant cooking—and one that's absolutely achievable at home. The combination of perfectly crispy salmon skin and silky French butter sauce is pure elegance.

## The Two Techniques That Matter

This dish is really about mastering two things: crispy skin salmon and classic beurre blanc. Let me break them down.

### Crispy Skin Salmon

The secret isn't complicated, but it requires patience:

**Dry the fish thoroughly.** Moisture is the enemy of crispy skin. Pat your salmon with paper towels multiple times until there's no moisture left on the surface.

**Start with a screaming hot pan.** A cold pan means the skin will stick and steam. Heat your pan for at least 2-3 minutes before adding oil.

**Don't touch it.** Once the salmon hits the pan, leave it alone. Pressing with a spatula for the first 30 seconds helps with contact, but after that, patience is key.

### Beurre Blanc: The Classic French Butter Sauce

Beurre blanc ("white butter") sounds fancy, but it's essentially an emulsion—cold butter whisked into a warm acid reduction. The key is temperature: too hot and the butter melts into grease; too cold and it won't emulsify.

The cream in this recipe acts as a stabilizer, making the sauce more forgiving. It's not strictly traditional, but it's what I recommend for home cooks making this for the first time.

## Why I Love This Dish

This is the dish I make when I want to impress someone without spending hours in the kitchen. Once you understand the techniques, it comes together in 30 minutes. The components can be prepped ahead: salmon dried and seasoned, butter cubed and chilled, shallots minced.

For a complete meal, serve alongside some simply steamed asparagus or a light salad. The richness of the sauce means you want something bright and fresh to balance it.

Place potatoes in a large pot and cover with cold water by 2 inches. Add 1 tablespoon of salt. Bring to a boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook until fork-tender, about 20-25 minutes.
Preheat your oven to 425°F (220°C). Line a large baking sheet with parchment paper and drizzle with 2 tablespoons of olive oil.
Drain the potatoes and let them cool for 5 minutes. Arrange them on the prepared baking sheet, leaving space between each potato.
Using the bottom of a glass or a potato masher, gently press down on each potato until it's about 1/2 inch thick. Some will break apart—that's fine and creates extra crispy bits.
Don't press too hard—you want them flattened but not completely mashed.

These are best served right out of the oven when they're at their crispiest. If you need to make them ahead, you can boil and smash the potatoes earlier in the day, then roast them just before serving.

We tested this recipe with both Yukon Gold and red potatoes. Both work great, but Yukon Golds get slightly crispier edges. We also tried using a wire rack for extra crispness, but found the parchment paper method produced nearly identical results with less cleanup.
For restaurant-level crispy potatoes, try the double-fry method: after smashing, refrigerate uncovered for an hour to dry out the surface, then roast. The drier surface means crispier results.

If there's one side dish that's earned a permanent spot in my weeknight rotation, it's these crispy smashed potatoes. They're the kind of recipe that makes people ask for seconds and assume you spent way more time in the kitchen than you actually did.

## Why This Recipe Works

The magic of smashed potatoes is in the technique. By boiling them first, you get that creamy, fluffy interior. Then smashing and roasting at high heat creates all those irresistible crispy edges and golden bits. It's the best of both worlds.

I've been making these for years, tweaking the recipe each time. The version you see here is the result of testing different potato varieties, oven temperatures, and herb combinations. Trust me when I say: this is the one.

## The Secret to Extra Crispy Edges

The crispiest smashed potatoes come down to three things:

1. **Dry potatoes**: After boiling, let them sit for a few minutes before smashing. The drier the surface, the crispier they'll get.

2. **Hot oil on the pan**: Drizzle oil on the baking sheet before adding the potatoes. This creates a frying effect on the bottom.

3. **Don't crowd them**: Give each potato room to breathe. Crowded potatoes steam instead of crisp.

## Make It Your Own

This basic recipe is endlessly adaptable. Here are some variations I love:

- **Parmesan version**: Add 1/4 cup grated Parmesan in the last 5 minutes of roasting
- **Spicy kick**: Add red pepper flakes with the herbs
- **Loaded style**: Top with sour cream, chives, and crumbled bacon
- **Mediterranean**: Use oregano instead of rosemary and top with crumbled feta

A professional chef's review of Georgia James in Houston, serving some of the best upscale Texas BBQ in the city.

As a chef, I'll admit I was skeptical of "upscale BBQ." The best brisket in Texas typically comes from pits behind gas stations, cooked by pitmasters who'd laugh at a wine list. But Georgia James made me a believer.

## What Sets It Apart

Georgia James comes from Chris Shepherd's Underbelly Hospitality group, and it shows. This isn't a pitmaster's passion project—it's a chef-driven restaurant that happens to focus on smoked meats. That means thoughtful sourcing (44 Farms beef, heritage pork), a real bar program, and service that doesn't involve standing in line for two hours.

But here's the thing: despite the fine dining trappings, the BBQ fundamentals are rock solid. The brisket comes from a proper offset smoker burning post oak. The bark is developed naturally, not rushed. The smoke ring is deep and genuine.

## The Brisket

Let me be direct: this is some of the best brisket I've eaten anywhere in Texas, and I don't say that lightly.

The fat cap is perfectly rendered—that's harder than it sounds with prime brisket, which has more marbling to begin with. The bark is aggressive but not bitter. The meat pulls apart with the slightest pressure while still holding together. And the smoke flavor is clean oak, not acrid or overpowering.

Is it worth $32 a pound? For special occasion BBQ in a sit-down restaurant with full service? Absolutely.

## The Beef Ribs

If the brisket is perfect, the beef ribs are absurd—in the best way. These are massive dinosaur bones coated in mahogany bark, with meat that jiggles like jello when you shake the bone.

One rib could feed two people, maybe three. The fat renders completely, basting the meat from within. This is BBQ at its most primal and satisfying.

## The One Miss

The potato salad was fine but forgettable. In a menu this strong, "fine" stands out as the weak link. It's a minor complaint—this isn't what you come here for anyway.

## The Verdict

Georgia James proves you can elevate BBQ without compromising what makes it great. The sourcing is impeccable, the technique is flawless, and the restaurant experience adds genuine value over standing in line at a traditional joint.

Is it expensive? Yes. Is it worth it for a celebration or a special night out? Without question. This is the BBQ restaurant I bring visiting chefs to when they ask about Houston's food scene.

An honest review of The Publican in Chicago's Fulton Market, featuring their legendary pork program and excellent oyster bar.

The Publican has been a Chicago institution since 2008, and fifteen years later, it's still one of the best reasons to fight for a reservation in Fulton Market. This beer-hall-meets-oyster-bar-meets-pork-temple remains essential eating.

## The Vibe

Walking into The Publican feels like entering a medieval great hall redesigned by someone with excellent taste. Long communal tables, exposed brick, and a general atmosphere of "we're all here to eat well" permeate the space. It's loud—sometimes uncomfortably so during peak hours—but that's part of the experience.

If you're planning an intimate conversation, look elsewhere. If you want to eat great pork and drink great beer with friends, this is your spot.

## What We Ate

### The Pork

Let's be clear: you come to The Publican for the pork. Their whole-hog program is legendary, and it shows in every dish.

The **country ham** is a perfect start—thinly sliced, slightly sweet, with enough funk to remind you this isn't grocery store deli meat. Paired with house pickles and good bread, it's an ideal first bite.

But the **pork belly** is the star. Impossibly crispy outside, meltingly tender inside, with an apple mostarda that cuts through the richness. I've had this dish on three separate visits, and it's never disappointed.

### The Oysters

The raw bar is legit. Six oysters from various regions, impeccably sourced and shucked. The selection changes frequently, and the staff knows their origins and flavor profiles. If you're an oyster person, you won't be disappointed.

### The Miss

The whole roasted fish was... fine. Well-executed technically, but at $42, I wanted more wow factor. It's a perfectly good dish that pales next to the pork program. For that price at The Publican, I'd rather get more ham and pork belly.

## The Beer

The Publican's beer list is one of Chicago's best, with a focus on Belgian and farmhouse styles. If you're not sure what to order, ask your server—they know the list well and can match a beer to your food.

## The Verdict

After all these years, The Publican still delivers. The pork program is worth the hype, the oysters are excellent, and the atmosphere (if you embrace the chaos) is genuinely fun. Skip the whole fish and lean into what they do best: pork and oysters, washed down with excellent beer.

A solid 4 out of 5—not quite perfect, but still one of my go-to recommendations for visitors asking "where should I eat in Chicago?"

The burger is America's most debated dish. Everyone has an opinion on patty thickness, cheese type, and toasting technique. So when we decided to do Chef vs. Home Cook, it had to be a burger.

## The Challenge

Each of us would make our ideal cheeseburger using our respective approaches. Xavier could use any technique and ingredient from his professional kitchen. Nick had to stick to what's available at a regular grocery store and use typical home equipment.

## Xavier's Approach

"A great burger starts with great beef," Xavier explains. "In restaurants, we control the blend—and that matters more than most people realize."

Xavier started with dry-aged ribeye and fresh chuck, grinding them together moments before cooking. The dry-aging adds a concentrated, almost nutty beef flavor, while the chuck provides the fat content needed for juiciness.

His patties were formed loosely (overworking develops gluten and makes burgers tough) and cooked on a flat-top at precisely 400°F, developing a beautiful crust while keeping the center a perfect medium-rare.

## Nick's Approach

"Look, I've made burgers with custom blends. They're great. But I've also made hundreds of burgers with grocery store ground beef, and you know what? They're also great."

Nick grabbed 80/20 ground chuck, seasoned generously with salt and pepper, and formed loose patties. His secret weapon: a screaming hot cast iron pan and the smash technique—pressing the patties thin for maximum crust.

"The Maillard reaction is your friend. More surface area means more crispy, beefy goodness."

## The Taste Test

We invited three unsuspecting friends to taste both burgers blind. The results?

**Xavier's burger:** "This tastes like... more. More beefy, more complex. Is this aged?"

**Nick's burger:** "This is exactly what I want when I crave a burger. Simple, satisfying, perfect."

Final preference was split 2-1 in favor of Xavier's burger, but everyone agreed both were excellent.

## What We Learned

The professional technique makes a measurable difference—but the home cook version proves you don't need fancy equipment or ingredients to make a genuinely great burger. The gap between "great" and "perfect" is much smaller than the gap between "okay" and "great."

If you only have 15 minutes and grocery store ingredients, Nick's approach delivers. If you have time and want to explore what's possible with beef, Xavier's method opens up new flavors.

That's really what this series is about: understanding when the extra effort pays off, and when simpler is just as good.
Why Mise en Place Matters (Even When It Doesn't)
A chef and a home cook debate whether prepping all your ingredients before cooking is essential—or just Instagram-worthy fussiness.
Small bowls of prepped ingredients arranged on a counter

In culinary school, mise en place—French for "everything in its place"—is treated as sacred. You prep every ingredient, measure every spice, and arrange everything in little bowls before you turn on a burner. The idea is simple: with everything ready, you can focus entirely on cooking.

Then I started cooking at home and had to do my own dishes.

## The Professional Reality

In a restaurant kitchen, mise en place isn't optional. When you're firing thirty covers during a rush, you don't have time to mince shallots. Everything must be within arm's reach, portioned, and ready to go. A missing ingredient doesn't just slow you down—it can crash your whole station.

But professional kitchens have prep cooks. Someone else chops those onions. Someone else portions the butter. The line cook who sautés your salmon never touched a cutting board.

## The Home Cook Reality

When Nick and I first cooked together, I instinctively started prepping everything before we began. He looked at me like I was wasting time.

"Why are you putting salt in a tiny bowl? It's salt. Just grab it when you need it."

He had a point. Some aspects of mise en place are pure habit, carried over from professional environments where they make sense but don't translate to home cooking.

## Where Nick Is Right

**You don't need everything in cute little bowls.** If you're sautéing onions and the next step is adding garlic, you can mince the garlic while the onions cook. That's not cutting corners—that's efficient time management.

**Some ingredients can be prepped on the fly.** If a recipe calls for "juice of one lemon," you can juice that lemon while something simmers. You don't need pre-juiced lemon waiting in a ramekin.

**Dishes matter.** Professional mise en place generates a mountain of prep containers. At home, that's your problem. Fewer dishes often means a better cooking experience.

## Where I'm Still Right

**Time-sensitive techniques need full attention.** If you're searing a steak, you need that butter and thyme ready immediately. You can't be digging through your spice cabinet while your $30 ribeye overcooks.

**Complicated dishes benefit from organization.** A stir-fry, where everything cooks in seconds, genuinely needs ingredients prepped and staged. Same with anything involving deglazing, where the pan is screaming hot and timing matters.

**Reading the full recipe first is non-negotiable.** This isn't technically mise en place, but the principle applies: know what's coming before you start. The worst surprise is discovering you need "rested, chilled dough" when you're about to start rolling.

## The Compromise

After years of cooking together, Nick and I have landed somewhere in the middle. I still prep more than he does—old habits—but I've relaxed about the bowl situation. He's learned to have time-sensitive ingredients ready before the heat goes on.

The goal isn't Instagram-worthy bowls of prepped ingredients. It's cooking without stress, without scrambling, without that moment of "oh no, where's the—"

Mise en place is a tool. Like any tool, it should serve you, not the other way around.

## The Practical Version

Here's how I'd adapt mise en place for home cooking:

1. **Read the recipe fully** before you start. Note any time-sensitive moments.

2. **Pre-prep only what's time-critical.** If you need to add five ingredients simultaneously, have those ready. If they're added over ten minutes of simmering, prep as you go.

3. **Group ingredients logically.** Pull everything from the fridge and pantry before starting. Even if you're not pre-chopping, knowing where everything is matters.

4. **Set up your workspace.** Clean cutting board, sharp knife, salt within reach, trash bowl nearby. This is mise en place at its core—organization that makes cooking flow.

5. **Accept imperfection.** Sometimes you'll realize mid-cook that you forgot something. It happens. The dish will probably still be good.

The little bowls are optional. The mindset of being prepared is not.
